subtopics.title: Scales: RF, plain and diagonal
subtopics.theory_md:
**Representative fraction** $RF=\dfrac{\text{length on drawing}}{\text{actual length}}$ (same units). Full size 1:1, reduction 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, enlargement 2:1, 5:1.

**Length of scale** $=RF\times$ maximum length to be measured.

A **plain scale** reads two units (e.g. m and dm); a **diagonal scale** reads three (m, dm, cm) because the diagonals split each small division into 10 more parts.

Diagonal scale: draw the length, divide into main divisions, sub-divide the left one into 10, erect a rectangle 10 divisions high, join the diagonals. Least count $=$ smallest division $/10$.
subtopics.basics_md: A scale is a ruler drawn smaller (or bigger) than the real thing. RF just says how many times smaller: 1/40 means the drawing is 40 times smaller.
key_points: RF = drawing length / actual length, both in the same unit
Length of scale = RF x maximum length
Plain scale reads two units, diagonal scale three
Diagonal scale: left division split into 10, 10 horizontals, diagonals give the third unit

questions.q: 1 cm on a map stands for 5 m on the ground. The RF is
A diagonal scale can read
questions.why: Main divisions, sub-divisions and the diagonal give three successive units (m, dm, cm).

questions.q: On a map 1 cm represents 2 km. Find the RF and the length of a plain scale needed to measure up to 12 km.
questions.model_answer_md:
$RF=\dfrac{1\ \text{cm}}{2\ \text{km}}=\dfrac{1}{2\times10^{5}}=\dfrac{1}{200000}$

Length of scale $=RF\times 12\ \text{km}=\dfrac{12\times10^{5}\ \text{cm}}{200000}=6$ cm.

Draw a 6 cm line, divide it into 6 parts of 1 cm (2 km each).
points: Length = RF x max length
6 cm, divided into 6 equal parts

questions.q: Explain why the diagonals of a diagonal scale read the third unit.
questions.model_answer_md:
The left main division (1 m) is split into 10 equal parts (dm) at the top and bottom. The height is split into 10 equal horizontal lines. The diagonal joins 0 at the bottom to the first dm mark at the top.

By **similar triangles**, on the $n$th horizontal line the diagonal has moved $n/10$ of one dm division. So each horizontal line adds one more cm (1/10 dm).
points: Left division and height both divided into 10
Similar triangles: the diagonal shifts 1/10 of a division per horizontal
So each horizontal line adds 1 cm
Length of scale = 6 m x 1/40 = 15 cm, six divisions of 2.5 cm
Left division split into 10 (dm), rectangle with 10 horizontals, diagonals
4.56 m = 4 m + 5 dm + 6 cm shown on the 6th horizontal line

subtopics.title: Conics and the ellipse
subtopics.theory_md:
A **conic** is the locus of a point whose distance from a **focus** bears a constant ratio (eccentricity $e$) to its distance from a **directrix**: ellipse $e<1$, parabola $e=1$, hyperbola $e>1$.

**Ellipse (foci definition):** $PF_1+PF_2=$ major axis $=2a$. With foci $2c$ apart, minor axis $=2\sqrt{a^2-c^2}$.

Methods: foci and arcs, concentric circles, rectangle (oblong), eccentricity.

**Tangent** at $P$: bisector of the external angle between $PF_1$ and $PF_2$. **Normal**: perpendicular to it at $P$ (bisects $\angle F_1PF_2$).
subtopics.basics_md: Pin two nails, tie a loop of string, pull it tight with a pencil and move round: that is an ellipse. The string length is the major axis.
key_points: Ellipse: sum of distances from the two foci is constant, equal to the major axis
Minor axis = 2 sqrt(a^2 - c^2)
e < 1 ellipse, e = 1 parabola, e > 1 hyperbola
Tangent bisects the external angle of the focal lines; normal is perpendicular to it

questions.q: The foci of an ellipse are 50 mm apart and the major axis is 70 mm. Find the minor axis.
questions.model_answer_md:
$2a=70\Rightarrow a=35$ mm; $2c=50\Rightarrow c=25$ mm.

Minor axis $=2\sqrt{a^2-c^2}=2\sqrt{35^2-25^2}=2\sqrt{600}=48.99\approx49.0$ mm.
points: Minor axis = 2 sqrt(a^2 - c^2)

questions.q: How are the tangent and normal drawn at a point P on an ellipse?
questions.model_answer_md:
1. Join $P$ to the foci $F_1$ and $F_2$.
2. Extend $F_1P$ beyond $P$. The bisector of the angle between $PF_2$ and this extension is the **tangent** at $P$.
3. The perpendicular to the tangent at $P$ (the bisector of $\angle F_1PF_2$) is the **normal**.
points: Join P to both foci
Bisector of the external angle is the tangent
Perpendicular to it at P is the normal
A and B are foci; AP + BP = 70 + 10 = 80 mm constant, so the curve is an ellipse
Major axis 80 mm, c = 30, minor axis 2 sqrt(40^2 - 30^2) = 52.9 mm

subtopics.title: Cycloid, epicycloid and hypocycloid
subtopics.theory_md:
A **cycloid** is the locus of a point on a circle rolling without slipping along a straight line. For one turn the base length is $\pi d$.

An **epicycloid** is traced when the circle rolls on the *outside* of a directing circle (radius $R$), a **hypocycloid** when it rolls on the *inside*. For one turn of the rolling circle (radius $r$) the centre moves through
$\theta=360^\circ\times\dfrac{r}{R}$.

Construction: divide the generating circle into 12; divide the path of its centre into 12; cut with radius $r$ from each centre.

**Normal** at a point: join it to the instantaneous contact point. **Tangent**: perpendicular to the normal.
subtopics.basics_md: Paint a dot on a wheel and roll it along the floor: the dot draws a cycloid. Roll the wheel round the outside of a drum and it is an epicycloid; round the inside, a hypocycloid.
key_points: Cycloid: rolls on a straight line, base length = pi d
Epicycloid outside, hypocycloid inside the directing circle
Angle for one turn: theta = 360 r / R
Normal passes through the contact point; tangent is perpendicular to it

questions.why: Rolling on the inside gives a hypocycloid; outside, an epicycloid.

Rolling on the outside gives an **epicycloid**.

$\theta=360^\circ\times\dfrac{r}{R}=360^\circ\times\dfrac{30}{120}=90^\circ$.

theta = 360 r / R
90 degrees

topics.topic: Types of lines, dimensioning and title block

subtopics.title: Types of lines and lettering
subtopics.theory_md:
Line types (IS 10714) and uses:
- **Continuous thick:** visible outlines and edges.
- **Continuous thin:** dimension, extension, projection and leader lines, hatching, construction lines.
- **Dashed (thin or medium):** hidden outlines and edges.
- **Chain thin:** centre lines, pitch circles.
- **Chain thin with thick ends and bends:** cutting planes.
- **Chain thin double-dashed:** adjacent parts, alternate positions.
- **Thin freehand or zigzag:** short or long break lines.

When lines coincide, the order is visible, hidden, centre.

**Lettering:** single-stroke capitals, vertical or inclined at $75^\circ$; heights 2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10 mm.
subtopics.basics_md: Different lines tell the reader different things: thick means you can see it, dashed means it is hidden behind, chain means axis or centre.
key_points: Visible edges: continuous thick; hidden edges: dashed
Centre lines: chain thin; cutting plane: chain thin, thick at ends
Dimension, extension and hatching lines are continuous thin
Priority when lines coincide: visible, then hidden, then centre
Lettering: single-stroke, vertical or 75 degrees

(Also: chain thin with thick ends for cutting planes; freehand wavy line for break.)

subtopics.title: Dimensioning rules and systems
subtopics.theory_md:
A dimension has **extension lines**, a **dimension line** with **arrowheads**, and the **figure** (in mm, no unit written). All are thin continuous lines; the figure is above the dimension line.

Rules:
- Extension lines start about 1 mm off the outline and go 2-3 mm beyond the dimension line.
- Never use an outline or centre line as a dimension line; do not repeat a dimension.
- Keep dimensions outside the view, smaller ones nearer the object.
- Arrowhead length about 3 times its width.
- Symbols: $\varnothing$ diameter, $R$ radius, $\square$ square.

Systems: **aligned** (text parallel to the line) and **unidirectional** (all text horizontal). Arrangements: chain, parallel, combined, coordinate.
subtopics.basics_md: Dimensions answer 'how big' and 'where': size dimensions give the sizes of features and location dimensions place them. Each should appear once, where the shape is clearest.
key_points: Thin continuous dimension and extension lines, arrowheads at ends
Figure in mm above the dimension line, no repeats
Extension lines 1 mm off the outline, 2-3 mm beyond the dimension line
Aligned and unidirectional systems; chain, parallel, combined, coordinate

**Rules**

2. Extension lines begin about 1 mm from the outline and extend 2-3 mm past the dimension line.
3. Do not use outlines or centre lines as dimension lines; avoid crossing lines.
4. Do not repeat a dimension; place it outside the view in mm without unit.

subtopics.title: Drawing sheets, border and title block
subtopics.theory_md:
Sheet sizes follow the A-series: each size is the previous one halved across its longer side, and sides are in the ratio $1:\sqrt2$. A0 is $841\times1189$ mm (area about $1\ \text{m}^2$); A1 $594\times841$; A2 $420\times594$; A3 $297\times420$; A4 $210\times297$.

A **border** (working area) is drawn in thick continuous lines inside the trimmed sheet. The **title block** sits at the bottom right corner, its bottom and right sides on the border. It carries drawing title, name, roll number, scale, projection symbol, date, sheet number, section/institute.
subtopics.basics_md: Every sheet is the same shape: cut A0 in half and you get two A1, cut A1 and you get A2. The title block is the label saying whose drawing it is.

subtopics.title: Drafting aids, layers and dimension styles
subtopics.theory_md:
Status-bar aids and keys: **GRID** (F7) shows dots, **SNAP** (F9) forces the cursor to grid steps, **ORTHO** (F8) locks to horizontal/vertical, **POLAR** (F10) locks to set angles, **OSNAP** (F3) picks exact points (endpoint, midpoint, centre, intersection, quadrant, tangent, perpendicular).

topics.topic: Theory of projections and reference planes

subtopics.title: Projection: elements and properties
subtopics.theory_md:
**Projection** is the image of an object formed on a plane by lines (**projectors**) drawn from its points. Four elements: the **object**, the **centre of projection** (station point or viewer), the **projectors**, and the **plane of projection**.

In **orthographic** projection the projectors are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the plane, which gives true shape and size where a face is parallel to the plane.

- A line or face parallel to the plane shows true length or true shape.
- Inclined to the plane: foreshortened.
- Perpendicular to the plane: a line shows as a point, a face as a line.
subtopics.basics_md: A shadow cast by the sun straight down on the ground is a projection. If the face is flat to the ground the shadow is its exact shape.
key_points: Elements: object, centre of projection, projectors, plane
Orthographic: parallel projectors perpendicular to the plane
Parallel to the plane: true size; inclined: shortened; perpendicular: point or line

questions.q: In orthographic projection the projectors are
options: parallel and perpendicular to the plane
parallel and inclined to the plane
questions.why: Parallel to each other and at right angles to the plane.

questions.why: All its projectors coincide, giving a point.

questions.q: Define projection and name its four elements. Why is orthographic projection used for working drawings?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Projection** is the image of an object on a plane obtained by projectors from its points.

**Elements:** object, centre of projection (viewer), projectors, plane of projection.

Orthographic projection is used because faces parallel to the plane keep their **true shape and size**, so dimensions can be read exactly.
points: Definition: image on a plane by projectors
Object, centre of projection, projectors, plane

subtopics.title: Reference planes and quadrants
subtopics.theory_md:
Two mutually perpendicular planes: the **Horizontal Plane (HP)** and **Vertical Plane (VP)**; their line of intersection is **XY**. A third, the **Profile Plane (PP)**, is perpendicular to both. HP and VP divide space into four **quadrants**: I (above HP, in front of VP), II (above, behind), III (below, behind), IV (below, in front).

The **front view** (elevation) is on the VP, the **top view** (plan) on the HP, the **side view** on the PP. To get both on one sheet, the HP is rotated $90^\circ$ **clockwise** about XY until it is in line with the VP.

Only the **first and third quadrants** are used, because in the second and fourth the two views overlap after rotation.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine standing in the corner of a room: the floor is the HP, the wall facing you is the VP. The space in front of the wall and above the floor is the first quadrant.
key_points: HP, VP and PP are mutually perpendicular; HP and VP meet in XY
Four quadrants; FV on VP, TV on HP, SV on PP
HP is rotated 90 degrees clockwise about XY
Only 1st and 3rd quadrants are used: views overlap in the 2nd and 4th

questions.q: A point lies above the HP and behind the VP. It is in the

questions.q: For an object in the third quadrant, the front view lies

questions.q: Explain how the front view and top view are shown on one flat sheet.
questions.model_answer_md:
The object is placed in the first quadrant. Its front view is projected on the **VP** and its top view on the **HP**.

The HP is then rotated **$90^\circ$ clockwise** about XY until it lies in the plane of the VP. The top view now falls **below XY** and the front view **above XY**, on the same projectors perpendicular to XY.

questions.q: Why are the second and fourth quadrants not used?
questions.model_answer_md: In the second and fourth quadrants, after the HP is rotated both views fall on the **same side of XY** and overlap, which makes the drawing confusing. The first and third quadrants keep the views on opposite sides of XY, hence **first-angle** and **third-angle** projection.

Only first and third angle projection are used

subtopics.title: Central, parallel and pictorial methods
subtopics.theory_md:
**Central (perspective)** projection: projectors meet at a point, the station point. Objects look realistic, nearer things appear larger and parallel lines converge at **vanishing points**; true dimensions are lost.

**Parallel** projection: the centre is at infinity, so the projectors are parallel. If the projectors are inclined to the plane it is **oblique**; if perpendicular it is **orthographic**.

Orthographic projection is *multiview* (two or more views on perpendicular planes) or *axonometric* (a single pictorial view: isometric, dimetric, trimetric).
subtopics.basics_md: Perspective is how a camera or eye sees (far things smaller). Parallel projection is as if the viewer were infinitely far away, so size does not shrink.
key_points: Perspective: projectors converge, realistic, vanishing points
Parallel: oblique (inclined) or orthographic (perpendicular)
Orthographic: multiview, or axonometric single pictorial view

questions.q: In perspective projection the projectors
options: are parallel and perpendicular to the plane

questions.q: Differentiate perspective, oblique and orthographic projections.
questions.model_answer_md:

subtopics.title: Isometric and oblique views
subtopics.theory_md:
**Axonometric** projection shows the object tilted so that three faces appear: **isometric** (all three axes equally foreshortened, axes $120^\circ$ apart, one vertical), **dimetric** (two equal), **trimetric** (none equal).

**Isometric scale** $=\sqrt{2/3}=0.816$, so isometric projection is $0.816$ times the true length; an **isometric drawing** uses true lengths and looks $1/0.816=1.225$ times larger. Circles become ellipses.

**Oblique** projection: the front face is true shape, the depth axis is drawn at $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$. **Cavalier:** depth full size. **Cabinet:** depth half size.
subtopics.basics_md: Isometric draws a cube with equal looking edges and a 120 degree star of axes. Oblique keeps the front face flat and just slides the depth back at an angle.
key_points: Isometric axes 120 degrees apart; isometric scale 0.816
Isometric drawing uses true lengths (1.225 times larger)
Dimetric: two angles equal; trimetric: none
Oblique: front face true shape; cavalier full depth, cabinet half depth

subtopics.title: First-angle layout and line conventions
subtopics.theory_md:
**First angle:** the object lies between the observer and the plane (observer, object, plane). The **front view** is on top; the **top view** is **below** it; the **left-hand side view** goes to the **right** of the front view and the **right-hand side view** to the **left**. **Third angle:** plane between observer and object; top view above, left view on the left.

subtopics.theory_md:
Method for a stepped block:
1. Fix the front view from the arrow; draw the **overall outline** of each view first from the overall length, height and depth.
2. Cut in the steps, notches and slots one by one, projecting every vertical edge from the FV down to the TV, and every horizontal edge across to the SV.
3. Depths come from the TV through a $45^\circ$ mitre line.
4. An edge that cannot be seen in a view is **dashed**; a step in the top face shows as a line in the FV and TV.

A **hole** shows as a **circle** in the view looking along its axis and as **two dashed lines** (its generators) in the views across it, with a **chain thin centre line** in each. A **counterbore** or spot-face shows as two concentric circles, and two dashed rectangles beside.

A rounded end (radius $R$) is an arc in the view along its axis; in the other views it is a rectangle with a tangent line where the arc meets the flat. Boss and lug heights come from the FV, the circle centre sits on the common centre line.

subtopics.title: Inclined faces, ribs and chamfers
subtopics.theory_md:
An **inclined face** is seen **edge-on** (a slanted line) in the view perpendicular to its slope direction, and as a **foreshortened surface** in the others. Its **true shape** appears only in a view perpendicular to it.

- A face perpendicular to the VP and inclined to the HP: slanted line in the FV, a rectangle in the TV and SV.
- A **rib** (web) is not hatched in a view; it shows as a triangle in the view across it.
- A **chamfer** at $45^\circ$ adds a line in the views where its edges are seen.

Project the two ends of every slanted edge from view to view; the line joining them gives the edge.
subtopics.basics_md: A slope is a tilted face. Look at it from the side and it is a slanted line; look from above and it is a plain rectangle (a bit shorter than its real length).

subtopics.title: Notation and position from the views
subtopics.theory_md:
Notation: actual point $A$, front view $a'$, top view $a$; both lie on one **projector** perpendicular to XY.

- Distance of $a'$ from XY $=$ distance of the point from the **HP**.
- Distance of $a$ from XY $=$ distance of the point from the **VP**.

| Quadrant | Position | $a'$ | $a$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | above HP, in front of VP | above XY | below XY |
| II | above HP, behind VP | above | above |
| III | below HP, behind VP | below | above |
| IV | below HP, in front of VP | below | below |

To read a position: front view above XY means above HP; top view below XY means in front of VP.
subtopics.basics_md: XY is the floor line of the wall. The front view tells you the height above or below the floor; the top view tells you how far in front of or behind the wall.

FV above XY: above HP; TV below XY: in front of VP
Q1 opposite sides, Q2 both above, Q3 opposite sides, Q4 both below

subtopics.theory_md:
Steps for a point given by its height $h$ and distance $d$:
1. Draw XY and a projector perpendicular to it (projectors are spaced as the question says).
2. **Front view $a'$:** $h$ above XY if above HP, below XY if below HP.
3. **Top view $a$:** $d$ **below** XY if in front of VP, **above** XY if behind VP.
4. Join $a$ and $a'$ by a thin projector; label correctly.

Mnemonic: *front view is height, top view is depth*. Quadrant I: $a'$ above, $a$ below. Quadrant II: both above. Quadrant III: $a'$ below, $a$ above. Quadrant IV: both below.

subtopics.title: Points in the HP, in the VP or in both
subtopics.theory_md:
A point **in the HP** has height $0$, so its **front view lies on XY** and its top view is at its distance from the VP.

A point **in the VP** has distance $0$, so its **top view lies on XY** and its front view is at its height.

A point in **both** planes lies on XY itself and both views coincide with it.

Such points sit on the boundary of two quadrants: in HP in front of VP (between I and IV), in HP behind VP (II and III), in VP above HP (I and II), in VP below HP (III and IV).
subtopics.basics_md: If a point lies on the floor its height is zero, so its front view sits right on XY. If it lies on the wall its distance is zero, so its top view sits on XY.
key_points: In HP: front view on XY
In VP: top view on XY
In both: both views on XY
Boundary points lie between two quadrants

subtopics.title: True distance between points and the room problems
subtopics.theory_md:
For two points whose projectors are $\Delta x$ apart, with difference in height $\Delta z$ and difference in distance from the VP $\Delta y$, the true distance is
$$PQ=\sqrt{\Delta x^2+\Delta y^2+\Delta z^2}.$$
If one point is above the HP and the other below, **add** the heights (and add the distances if one is in front of and the other behind the VP).

Graphically: the top-view length gives $\Delta x,\Delta y$; rotate it parallel to XY and join with the height difference to get the true length.

For a room, treat each object and corner as a point: the walls are the planes, the floor is the HP, the end wall the VP.
subtopics.basics_md: It is just the 3-D Pythagoras: how far across, how far along, how far up, combined.
key_points: PQ = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)
Add distances when points lie on opposite sides of HP or VP
Treat objects as points; scale 1 m = 1 cm and so on
Different quadrants: views on both sides of XY
